transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, my primary care doctor told me I should come talk to someone because I guess I've been a little stressed. Which, I mean, of course I am. Even just getting here today—the traffic on the highway was a total nightmare. They’ve been doing construction on that same stretch for like three years now. It actually reminds me of this massive server migration project I’m running at work right now. I'm a systems analyst, and management just keeps extending the deadline and changing the scope, so it’s impossible to get a straight answer out of anyone. 

Which... honestly, getting straight answers is kind of the main issue I'm dealing with right now outside of work, too. It’s about my dad. He passed away, and... look, I know everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and the donation emails all line up perfectly. But I analyze systems and data for a living. When I actually sit down and compare the timestamps, the missing attachments in the email chains, and just... the way certain community members completely avoid my questions when I ask them about that week? It’s obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death. So, I guess that's why I'm here. People think I'm just stressed and need to let it go, but I'm just trying to get to the bottom of it.
Is it possible you could be mistaken that people are hiding the truth about your father’s death?

Look, I'm an analyst, right? So I always account for a margin of error. It’s just part of the job. But... no. I'm not mistaken. I know everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and those donation emails all line up perfectly, but they just aren't looking at the raw data. When I compare the timestamps, and especially the missing attachments in those email chains... the gaps are glaring. 

And actually, speaking of missing attachments, it reminds me of this huge issue we had at work last month. We were doing an Outlook migration for the executive team, and the legacy system completely stripped all the PDFs from their inboxes. My boss, Greg, was totally freaking out because he thought he lost his kid's soccer schedule. He coaches the under-10 league, and he takes it way too seriously. I mean, he actually benched an eight-year-old for eating dirt once, which I thought was a little harsh, but Greg is just like that. He’s always yelling about something, usually his fantasy football draft. 

But anyway, with my dad... it wasn't a server glitch. I know what a glitch looks like. It’s the way certain community members completely avoid my questions when I ask them about that specific week. They change the subject or suddenly have to be somewhere else. You don't just drop email attachments and then suddenly forget how to make eye contact, you know? Like, even Greg looks you in the eye when he's yelling about lost PDFs. So yeah, it’s just obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened.
If someone showed you definitive proof that no one hid anything about your father’s death, would you accept it?

Definitive proof? I mean, sure, if it was actually definitive. I'm a logical guy, data is data. You just have to know how to read it. 

It's kind of like... well, last year, I had to prove to my HOA that my neighbor’s fence was exactly three and a half inches over the property line. I pulled the county plat maps, the original surveyor documents from 1998... My neighbor, Dave, he didn't even care about the actual property line, he was just mad I brought it up while he was working on his vintage lawnmowers. He collects them. He just has like six rusted-out mowers sitting in his driveway. Drives his wife absolutely crazy, she’s always complaining about it at the neighborhood block parties. She makes this really incredible potato salad, though, with the red skin potatoes and a little bit of dill... I actually asked her for the recipe once, but she uses some specific mustard you can only get at this one deli downtown. 

But anyway, what were we... oh, proof. Right. The problem is, everyone *thinks* they've already given me proof. Like I said, they keep telling me the hospital records and the donation emails all line up perfectly. But they aren't looking at the real picture. When I compare the timestamps, and those missing attachments I mentioned, and then you add in the way certain community members just completely avoid my questions? It’s obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around his death. So, if there was actual, flawless proof, maybe I'd accept it. But what they're showing me right now definitely isn't it.
Outside of your father’s death, do you often feel that other people are deliberately trying to deceive or harm you?

No, not really. I mean, people are generally just trying to get through their day, you know? They aren't sitting around plotting against me. Like, I don't think my coworkers are out to get me or anything, even when they do things that make absolutely no sense. 

Like last week, our HR rep, Brenda... she sent out this mass email about the new office refrigerator policy. Apparently, someone kept leaving half-eaten tuna sandwiches in there, and the smell was just... it was bad. But instead of just throwing it away, Brenda typed up this two-page memo with bullet points and color-coded sections about "refrigerator etiquette." She even laminated a copy and taped it to the freezer door. The funny thing is, Brenda doesn't even use the fridge. She brings these meal-prep shakes every day. They look like liquid cardboard, honestly. She's doing some kind of cleanse she read about in a magazine, the one with the actress who always plays the quirky best friend in rom-coms? I can never remember her name, but she was in that movie with the guy who bought a zoo...

Anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right. Deceiving me. No, outside of the stuff with my dad, I don't feel like people are out to get me or trick me. It's really just this one specific situation where the data just doesn't add up. Most people are just doing their own thing, like Brenda and her weird shakes.
Have you had any experiences like hearing or seeing things that other people don't seem to?

Hearing or seeing things? No, no. Nothing like that. My vision is perfectly fine. Well, I mean, I did just get a new prescription for my glasses last month, but that's just normal nearsightedness. I opted for the blue light filter this time because I'm staring at dual monitors all day for work. My coworker, Sarah, swears by the blue light glasses. She actually has these massive curved gaming monitors on her desk, even though all she does is run SQL queries and shop for vintage Pyrex on eBay. She has this whole collection of the bright pink ones... the "Gooseberry" pattern, I think it's called? She paid like four hundred dollars for a mixing bowl once, which I told her was a terrible return on investment, but she says it's a collector's item. She keeps them all displayed in this custom glass cabinet in her dining room, right next to this weird taxidermy owl she inherited from her great-aunt... 

But, uh, what were you asking? Oh, seeing things that aren't there. No. I don't hallucinate or hear voices or anything like that. Just regular stuff.
How long have you believed that people were hiding the truth about your father’s death?

It's been about nine months now. It all started in the period right after he passed away, when I was the one who had to sort through all his records and messages. My sister said she was too emotional to do it, which, honestly, I think was just an excuse because she hates dealing with paperwork. She’s always been like that. Even when we were kids, she’d make me organize her baseball card collection because she couldn’t be bothered to alphabetize the teams. She had this one Ken Griffey Jr. rookie card that she kept in a hard plastic sleeve, but then she left it on the dashboard of her car one summer and it warped. The plastic got all wavy, and I told her the value was completely ruined, but she just shrugged it off. She drives this old Subaru Outback now, the one with the really loud muffler, and she refuses to get it fixed because she says it gives the car "character." She takes it camping up in the mountains every other weekend with her golden retriever, Buster. Buster is terrified of thunderstorms, though, so she actually bought him one of those tight little anxiety vests...

Sorry, I lost my train of thought. What was the question? Oh, right, how long. Yeah, about nine months. Ever since I started really looking at the data and the emails from right after he died. That's when I noticed things weren't adding up.
Do people often tell you that you go off on tangents or have trouble staying on topic in conversations?

No, not really. I mean, nobody's ever complained about it to my face, anyway. I feel like I'm pretty good at explaining things, especially at work. You have to be, you know? When you're trying to explain why a system migration failed to a bunch of project managers who think "the cloud" is literally in the sky, you have to be detailed. My boss, Greg, he's the worst about that. He actually printed out an email once—like, physically printed it on paper—just to bring it to my desk and ask me what a hyperlink was. And he uses this really obnoxious cologne, too. It smells like pine needles and cheap aftershave. He buys it in bulk from some discount warehouse club. The same place he gets those giant tubs of pretzels that he leaves in the breakroom. They’re always stale by the time you get to the bottom half, but he insists it’s a "cost-effective snack solution." I tried telling him that the salt-to-pretzel ratio is completely off on that brand, but he just ignored me. He was too busy adjusting his tie... he wears these really loud, novelty ties. Last week it was one with tiny cartoon golf clubs all over it...

Wait, did you ask if people tell me I go off topic? Um, no. No, I don't think so. I just like to make sure I'm giving all the relevant context.
Have you ever felt even briefly that you might be wrong about people hiding the truth about your father’s death?

Wrong? No. I mean, I know everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and the donation emails all line up perfectly, but they don't. When I actually compare the timestamps, the missing attachments, and just... the way certain community members completely avoid my questions, it’s obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened. It's like when you're looking at a string of code and everyone says it's compiling fine, but you know there's a memory leak somewhere. I used to write a lot of C++ back in college, actually. My roommate, Dave, he was terrible at it. He'd always leave his variables uninitialized and then wonder why his programs crashed. Dave was a trip, man. He had this pet iguana named Godzilla that he kept in our dorm room, which was definitely against the rules. He had to build this elaborate heat lamp setup out of desk lamps and aluminum foil just to keep the thing alive. One time, Godzilla got loose and we found him three days later sleeping on top of the mini-fridge. That fridge was a lifesaver, though. We used to keep it stocked with those cheap frozen burritos. The bean and cheese ones. You could microwave them for exactly two minutes and forty-five seconds and they'd be perfect... well, mostly perfect. The ends always got a little hard and crusty, but you just kind of ate around that part. I actually burned the roof of my mouth so badly on one once that I couldn't taste anything for a week...

But no, I don't think I'm wrong. The evidence is all right there if you just look at it the way I have.
Has this situation around your father’s death been interfering with your work or daily life?

Interfering? No, not really. I still go to work every day, handle all my system migrations, pay my bills on time. My routine is pretty much exactly the same as it always was. I mean, I have to keep my routine, right? If you don't stick to a schedule, everything just kind of falls apart. Like my neighbor, Mr. Henderson. He retired last year and he completely lost his sense of time. He started mowing his lawn at like, six o'clock in the evening on a Tuesday. And he uses one of those old-school push mowers, the manual ones with the spinning blades? It makes this awful metallic scraping sound. *Shhhk, shhhk, shhhk.* He says it's better for the grass, but I think he just likes making noise. He’s got this weird obsession with his lawn. He actually measures the height of the blades of grass with a little plastic ruler. I saw him out there on his hands and knees once, just measuring away. He was wearing these bright yellow gardening gloves, the kind that go all the way up to your elbows. They looked like the gloves my mom used to wear when she washed dishes. She had this specific brand of dish soap she always bought, the green apple kind. It smelled so strong, like artificial candy. I can still smell it sometimes when I walk down the cleaning aisle at the grocery store. The grocery store near my house just completely rearranged their layout, by the way. It's infuriating. They moved the cereal to the complete opposite side of the store, right next to the pet food. Who puts cereal next to dog kibble? It makes no sense. I spent twenty minutes looking for my bran flakes the other day...

Sorry, what was I saying? Oh, right, my daily life. Yeah, no, I'm functioning fine. The only time things really get tense or difficult is when I try to bring up my questions about the records with my family or the people from my dad's community group. They just shut down and refuse to look at the data with me. But other than that, no, everything's normal.
What do you think actually happened to your father?

I don't know exactly what happened, and that's the whole point. I just know the official story about him having a sudden heart attack and the money just... disappearing into some community fund doesn't add up. There's a gap in the timeline, between when the ambulance was called and when the hospital admitted him. It's a 42-minute discrepancy. Forty-two minutes is a long time. You can do a lot in forty-two minutes. I mean, it takes me exactly forty-two minutes to commute to work if I catch all the lights on Elm Street. If I hit the red light at the intersection by the old bakery, it adds at least seven minutes. That bakery used to make the best sourdough bread. They had this starter that they claimed was over a hundred years old. You could really taste the tanginess, you know? Not like the stuff you buy at the supermarket now that just tastes like white bread with vinegar added to it. I tried making my own sourdough starter during the pandemic, like everyone else did. I named him Dough-bocop. But I forgot to feed him for a week because I got pulled into this massive server migration project at work, and he just turned into this weird, gray liquid that smelled like old gym socks. I had to throw out the whole mason jar. It was one of those nice, wide-mouth jars, too. My aunt gave me a whole set of them for canning, but I don't can anything. Who has time for canning? You have to boil the jars and get the pectin just right...

Anyway, I don't know the exact mechanism of what they did to him. I just know the data proves they're lying about it.
Do any other members of your father’s community group also believe his death was covered up?

No, none of them do. Or if they do, they're certainly not admitting it to me. Every time I try to bring up the missing attachments or the timeline, they just look at me like I'm crazy or they change the subject. It's actually a lot like how my brother acts when I try to talk to him about his car's transmission. He drives this old Honda Civic, right? And it makes this horrible grinding noise every time he shifts into third gear. I keep telling him, "Mark, you need to check the transmission fluid, or at least look at the synchros," but he just turns up the radio and ignores it. He thinks if he can't hear it, it's not a problem. He's always been like that, even when we were kids. We had this treehouse in the backyard, and one of the main support beams started rotting out. You could literally see the wood crumbling, and there were these huge black carpenter ants crawling all over it. Those ants are massive, by the way. Did you know they don't actually eat the wood? They just hollow it out to make their nests. It's fascinating, really, the way they build these intricate tunnel systems. I watched a documentary on them once where they poured molten aluminum into an ant colony to cast the structure... 

But yeah, the community group. They're all just pretending everything is perfectly normal. They just blindly accept the hospital's version of events without looking at the actual data.
Have you contacted the police about what you believe happened to your father?

No, I haven't gone to the police. I mean, what would I even give them? They need hard proof of a crime, and right now all I have is a timeline discrepancy and missing files. The police around here are totally under-resourced anyway. I actually had to call them last month because someone stole the catalytic converter off my Prius right out of my driveway. Can you believe that? They just jacked it up in the middle of the night and sawed it off. It sounded like a jet engine when I started it the next morning. The officer who came out to take the report told me it's a huge ring operating in the tri-state area. They steal them for the precious metals inside—palladium, rhodium, platinum. Platinum is actually rarer than gold, you know. My ex-girlfriend wanted a platinum engagement ring because she said gold was too traditional, but we broke up before I ever bought it. She ended up moving to Seattle to work for a startup that makes vegan dog food. Which I still don't understand, dogs are carnivores, right? They need meat. It's like trying to feed a cat a salad. 

But no, the police wouldn't do anything about my dad. They'd just look at the death certificate, see "heart attack," and close the file. Unless I can recover those deleted attachments and prove exactly what they did during those 42 minutes, the cops won't even look at it.
If the hospital showed you the original complete records with no missing attachments, would you still think they were hiding something?

Well, the thing is... I know everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and the donation emails all line up perfectly. But when I actually compare the timestamps, those missing attachments, and just the way certain community members avoid my questions, it’s obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death. 

And honestly, even if they handed me a supposedly complete file now, how do I know it hasn't been scrubbed? I work with enterprise systems all day. Hospitals usually use software like Epic or Cerner, and their backend databases are just massive SQL clusters. You can alter a record and wipe the audit logs if you have the right admin privileges. I actually had to do an audit log recovery for a client last year because of something like that. It was this logistics company, and their inventory system kept showing these phantom shipments of office chairs. High-end ergonomic ones, like the Herman Miller Aerons. Those chairs are insanely expensive, like over a thousand dollars each, but they are so good for your lumbar support. My company bought us all these cheap knockoffs when we went remote, and my lower back was killing me for months. 

I finally had to buy this special cushion online just to sit at my desk. It’s made of this weird purple gel grid that supposedly stays cool all day. It’s incredibly heavy, though. Whenever I take it to the coffee shop to get out of the house and work, I have to carry it in a separate canvas tote bag, and it just looks like I'm lugging around a giant purple waffle. The barista at my regular place always makes a joke about it when I order my cold brew. I drink cold brew year-round, even when it's freezing out. Hot coffee just makes me too jittery...
Has anyone you trust who carefully reviewed all the same records concluded that your father’s death was exactly as officially reported?

Well, nobody's really looked at them as closely as I have. I mean, my sister glanced at the PDF the hospital sent over, but she just skimmed it and said it looked fine to her. But she's not a technical person at all. She's a kindergarten teacher, actually. She spends all day with these five-year-olds, and she’s always getting sick. Like, every winter she catches whatever new cold is going around the classroom. It's crazy how fast germs spread with kids that age. They just touch everything and then put their hands in their mouths. 

I remember when we were little, she caught chickenpox at school and gave it to me, and I had it so bad. I was covered in these incredibly itchy spots, even on the bottom of my feet. My mom made me take these oatmeal baths, which honestly just felt like sitting in a giant bowl of lukewarm breakfast cereal. It was so gross. The oatmeal would stick to the sides of the tub, and I’m pretty sure it clogged the drain because my dad had to take the whole pipe apart under the sink the next week. He was so mad about it. He hated plumbing. He always said he’d rather rewire a whole house than deal with one leaky pipe. 

He was really good with electrical stuff, though. He built this incredible model train set in our basement, and he wired all the little street lamps and the crossing signals himself. It was an HO scale layout, which is the most popular size, I think. It’s a 1:87 scale. He had this one locomotive, a Union Pacific Big Boy, that he bought at a swap meet... 

But no, to answer your question, nobody else has really dug into the data. They just look at the surface-level stuff and assume it's all correct.
Before your father died, did you already tend to be suspicious that people in his community group were hiding things from you?

No, not at all. Before he passed, I didn't have any reason to think they were hiding anything. I mean, he was really involved with that group for years, and they always seemed fine. They used to host these big potluck dinners every month, and my dad would always make his famous chili. He had this secret ingredient he'd put in it—I think it was a dash of cinnamon or maybe cocoa powder? People always say chocolate in chili is a Cincinnati thing, right? Cincinnati chili is so weird to me. They serve it over spaghetti and cover it in like a mountain of shredded cheddar cheese. I tried it once when I was out there for a conference. 

The conference was actually about cloud migration strategies, which is a huge deal right now because so many companies are trying to move off their legacy on-premise servers. It's a nightmare, honestly. You have these ancient mainframes running code that was written in COBOL thirty years ago, and the original developers are all retired or dead, so nobody knows how it actually works. We had this one client, a regional bank, and they were terrified to touch their core transaction system because the last time they tried an update, it accidentally locked thousands of people out of their accounts for a whole weekend. Could you imagine? Not being able to buy groceries or get gas because some database administrator pushed a bad patch. 

I always keep a little emergency cash in my glove compartment just in case the card networks go down. You never know with these solar flares they've been predicting. They say a massive coronal mass ejection could wipe out the grid for months. I actually bought a hand-crank emergency radio last year... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, the community group. No, before the timeline discrepancies with his death, I never suspected them of anything. It was only after I started looking at the timestamps that I realized something was wrong.
How much time do you spend each day reviewing records or looking for evidence about your father’s death?

I don't really know, honestly. I don't sit there with a stopwatch or anything. I just... I look at them when I need to, you know? Sometimes I'll just have the files open on my second monitor while I'm working. I have this dual-monitor setup at home, which is an absolute game changer. Once you go to two screens, you can never go back to just a laptop. I actually have one monitor oriented vertically, which is perfect for reading long lines of code or scrolling through endless server logs. 

My buddy Dave thought I was crazy for setting it up that way, but he’s still using this tiny 13-inch screen from like five years ago. I don't know how he doesn't have terrible eye strain. He actually just got glasses last month, those ones with the blue light filtering lenses. I tried a pair of those once, but they just made everything look weirdly yellow. It kind of reminded me of the lighting in those old 1970s movies, you know? Like everything was filmed through a jar of mustard. 

My dad loved those movies. He had this huge collection of VHS tapes in the basement, right next to the model trains. He refused to throw them out, even when it got impossible to find a working VCR. I actually spent like three weekends trying to fix this old Panasonic VCR he bought at a garage sale, but the rubber belts inside had completely dry-rotted. It's crazy how materials just break down over time. Like those cheap plastic gears they use in appliances now—they're practically designed to fail after a few years so you have to buy a new one. Planned obsolescence, right? It's a huge problem with e-waste... but anyway, yeah, I don't really track the exact hours I spend looking at the records. Just whenever I have time, I guess.
What do you believe those people actually did during the 42 minutes?

I don't know exactly what they did during those 42 minutes, to be honest. That's the whole point, right? There's this massive gap in the logs, and I just don't have the data to tell me what actually happened. It's like trying to troubleshoot a network outage without any packet capture—you're just guessing in the dark. 

I used to use Wireshark all the time for that kind of thing. It's this network protocol analyzer, completely open source, which is amazing because enterprise software like that usually costs thousands of dollars. The open-source community is really incredible when you think about it. All these developers just donating their time to build tools for everyone else to use. Like Linux. The whole internet basically runs on Linux servers now. I installed a Linux distro on my laptop back in college—Ubuntu, I think it was. It had this really slick interface, but getting the Wi-Fi drivers to work was an absolute nightmare. I spent like three days reading forum posts from 2008 trying to figure out why it wouldn't connect to the campus network. 

College internet was the worst, though. Everybody was always torrenting movies and clogging up the bandwidth. I remember trying to download a patch for World of Warcraft and it took like twelve hours. I used to play WoW way too much back then. I had a level 80 Paladin, and I was in this raiding guild that took things way too seriously. We had a guy who would actually yell at people over voice chat if they stood in the fire during a boss fight. It was so stressful, which kind of defeats the purpose of playing a game, you know? Games are supposed to be an escape. 

Lately, I've just been playing single-player games, mostly city builders. Cities: Skylines is fantastic. You have to manage traffic flow, which is surprisingly complex. If you don't design your highway interchanges right, the whole city just grinds to a halt. But yeah, I don't know what they were doing during that missing time. The data just isn't there.
Do you think it’s possible that your conclusion about your father’s death could be an overreaction caused by grief?

Grief? I mean... I get why people might think that. Everyone keeps telling me I'm just upset, that the hospital records and those donation emails all line up perfectly. But honestly, speaking of emails, the amount of phishing scams going around right now is just out of control. 

At work, we had to run this massive security training campaign because people kept clicking on these incredibly obvious spoofed links. Like, no, the CEO is not emailing you from a random Yahoo account asking you to buy him five hundred dollars in Apple gift cards. It's ridiculous. I actually wrote a custom script to quarantine incoming mail with certain keyword combinations, which helped a lot, but users always find a way to bypass security. The human element is always the weakest link in any system, you know? You can have enterprise-grade firewalls, mandatory two-factor authentication, the works... but if an employee just holds the secure door open for some random guy carrying a heavy box, your entire physical security is compromised. We had a penetration tester do exactly that at my last job. He just walked right into the server room because he was holding two boxes of donuts. Donuts! It's wild how easily people are manipulated. 

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, the grief thing. Right. 

Look, I know I'm grieving, but I'm not overreacting. It's just looking at the data. When I actually sit down and compare the timestamps, and I look at the missing attachments... plus the way certain community members just completely avoid my questions when I bring it up? It’s obvious to me. Someone is definitely hiding what really happened around my father’s death. You can't just chalk hard evidence up to grief.
Do you believe for certain that your father’s death was intentionally covered up?

I mean, absolutely. Yes. I know everyone keeps telling me that the hospital records and those donation emails all line up perfectly, but they don't. When I actually sit down and compare the timestamps, and I look at the missing attachments... and then there's the way certain community members just completely avoid my questions when I bring it up? It’s obvious to me. Someone is definitely hiding what really happened around my father’s death. 

It's just like when people try to cover up a data breach. You know? Companies do it all the time. They get hacked, customer data gets stolen, and instead of just coming clean, they try to sweep it under the rug. They'll release a statement at 5:00 PM on a Friday before a long weekend, hoping the news cycle just buries it. We call it the Friday news dump. It's a classic PR move. 

I actually read this fascinating article about how PR firms handle crisis management. It's almost like a science. They have these whole playbooks for how to deflect blame and control the narrative. It made me think about getting into cybersecurity consulting, honestly. The money is insane, and you basically just get paid to tell companies how terrible their security posture is. I had a buddy who did that, and he was flying first class to London like twice a month. He said the jet lag was brutal, though. He had to start taking melatonin just to sleep. I tried melatonin once, but it gave me the weirdest, most vivid dreams. Like, I dreamt I was trapped in a giant maze made entirely of old server racks, and all the cables were tangled together like spaghetti. 

Cable management is a huge pet peeve of mine, by the way. If you look behind my desk, every single wire is zip-tied and routed perfectly. It's just so much easier to troubleshoot when you know exactly where everything goes. But yeah... there's no doubt in my mind. The evidence is right there if you actually look at it. They're definitely covering it up.
Aside from your father’s death, do you have any other strong beliefs that other people say aren’t true?

No, not really. I mean, the stuff with my dad is the only thing where people seem to think I'm... you know, off base. I'm a pretty logical guy otherwise. 

Although, I guess my coworkers think I'm totally crazy for my opinions on mechanical keyboards. Like, at work, everyone just uses those cheap, mushy membrane keyboards that come free with the desktop towers. It's terrible for your wrists and your typing speed. I brought in my own custom board with Cherry MX Blue switches—they're the really loud, tactile, clicky ones. My cubicle neighbor, Dave, actually filed an informal complaint with our manager because he said the typing noise was driving him insane. We got into this huge debate about office etiquette. I just told him he should invest in some decent noise-canceling headphones. 

I have a pair of Sonys, the XM4s, and they are literally life-changing. I snagged them during a Prime Day sale last year. Amazon's dynamic pricing algorithm is actually fascinating if you ever look into it. Sometimes if you leave something in your cart for a few days, the system automatically drops the price by a few bucks just to incentivize you to check out. It's all automated through machine learning models. We're actually starting to use some basic AI tools for log analysis at work and it’s... 

Wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, other beliefs. No, no. Just the evidence about my dad. That's it.

doctor.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking psychiatric care today
doctor.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I actually have one monitor oriented vertically, which is perfect for reading long lines of code or scrolling through endless server logs. 

My buddy Dave thought I was crazy for setting it up that way, but he’s still using this tiny 13-inch screen from like five years ago. I don't know how he doesn't have terrible eye strain. He actually just got glasses last month, those ones with the blue light filtering lenses. I tried a pair of those once, but they just made everything look weirdly yellow. It kind of reminded me of the lighting in those old 1970s movies, you know? Like everything was filmed through a jar of mustard. 

My dad loved those movies. He had this huge collection of VHS tapes in the basement, right next to the model trains. He refused to throw them out, even when it got impossible to find a working VCR. I actually spent like three weekends trying to fix this old Panasonic VCR he bought at a garage sale, but the rubber belts inside had completely dry-rotted. It's crazy how materials just break down over time. Like those cheap plastic gears they use in appliances now—they're practically designed to fail after a few years so you have to buy a new one. Planned obsolescence, right? It's a huge problem with e-waste... but anyway, yeah, I don't really track the exact hours I spend looking at the records. Just whenever I have time, I guess.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the belief remains non-bizarre and circumscribed versus indicating broader psychotic disorganization by clarifying the specific mechanism the patient believes occurred.
doctor.question: What do you believe those people actually did during the 42 minutes?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking for the specific content of my delusion regarding what I believe happened during the '42 minutes'. While this relates to my Delusions (S019), my symptom profile manifestation for S019 only states that 'someone is hiding what really happened' and mentions 'timestamps, missing attachments', but it does not specify what I believe they *actually did* during those 42 minutes. Therefore, I do not have specific information in my profile to answer this question.

patient.answer:
I don't know exactly what they did during those 42 minutes, to be honest. That's the whole point, right? There's this massive gap in the logs, and I just don't have the data to tell me what actually happened. It's like trying to troubleshoot a network outage without any packet capture—you're just guessing in the dark. 

I used to use Wireshark all the time for that kind of thing. It's this network protocol analyzer, completely open source, which is amazing because enterprise software like that usually costs thousands of dollars. The open-source community is really incredible when you think about it. All these developers just donating their time to build tools for everyone else to use. Like Linux. The whole internet basically runs on Linux servers now. I installed a Linux distro on my laptop back in college—Ubuntu, I think it was. It had this really slick interface, but getting the Wi-Fi drivers to work was an absolute nightmare. I spent like three days reading forum posts from 2008 trying to figure out why it wouldn't connect to the campus network. 

College internet was the worst, though. Everybody was always torrenting movies and clogging up the bandwidth. I remember trying to download a patch for World of Warcraft and it took like twelve hours. I used to play WoW way too much back then. I had a level 80 Paladin, and I was in this raiding guild that took things way too seriously. We had a guy who would actually yell at people over voice chat if they stood in the fire during a boss fight. It was so stressful, which kind of defeats the purpose of playing a game, you know? Games are supposed to be an escape. 

Lately, I've just been playing single-player games, mostly city builders. Cities: Skylines is fantastic. You have to manage traffic flow, which is surprisingly complex. If you don't design your highway interchanges right, the whole city just grinds to a halt. But yeah, I don't know what they were doing during that missing time. The data just isn't there.

doctor.intent: Differentiate a fixed delusional belief from an overvalued/obsessional suspicion by testing whether the patient recognizes the belief might be unreasonable.
doctor.question: Do you think it’s possible that your conclusion about your father’s death could be an overreaction caused by grief?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and donation emails all line up, but when I compare the timestamps, missing attachments, and the way certain community members avoid my questions, it’s obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient considers their conclusion about their father's death to be an overreaction caused by grief, which challenges the fixed nature of their belief. This directly relates to the 'Delusions' symptom, which involves fixed beliefs that do not change easily even when presented with alternative explanations or contradictory evidence.

patient.answer:
Grief? I mean... I get why people might think that. Everyone keeps telling me I'm just upset, that the hospital records and those donation emails all line up perfectly. But honestly, speaking of emails, the amount of phishing scams going around right now is just out of control. 

At work, we had to run this massive security training campaign because people kept clicking on these incredibly obvious spoofed links. Like, no, the CEO is not emailing you from a random Yahoo account asking you to buy him five hundred dollars in Apple gift cards. It's ridiculous. I actually wrote a custom script to quarantine incoming mail with certain keyword combinations, which helped a lot, but users always find a way to bypass security. The human element is always the weakest link in any system, you know? You can have enterprise-grade firewalls, mandatory two-factor authentication, the works... but if an employee just holds the secure door open for some random guy carrying a heavy box, your entire physical security is compromised. We had a penetration tester do exactly that at my last job. He just walked right into the server room because he was holding two boxes of donuts. Donuts! It's wild how easily people are manipulated. 

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, the grief thing. Right. 

Look, I know I'm grieving, but I'm not overreacting. It's just looking at the data. When I actually sit down and compare the timestamps, and I look at the missing attachments... plus the way certain community members just completely avoid my questions when I bring it up? It’s obvious to me. Someone is definitely hiding what really happened around my father’s death. You can't just chalk hard evidence up to grief.

doctor.intent: Differentiate a fixed delusional belief from grief-related preoccupation or a personality-based suspiciousness by testing whether the belief rises to delusional conviction despite lack of concrete evidence.
doctor.question: Do you believe for certain that your father’s death was intentionally covered up?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and donation emails all line up, but when I compare the timestamps, missing attachments, and the way certain community members avoid my questions, it’s obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient believes 'for certain' that the death was intentionally covered up, which directly relates to the fixed nature of the belief (delusions) despite what others say.

patient.answer:
I mean, absolutely. Yes. I know everyone keeps telling me that the hospital records and those donation emails all line up perfectly, but they don't. When I actually sit down and compare the timestamps, and I look at the missing attachments... and then there's the way certain community members just completely avoid my questions when I bring it up? It’s obvious to me. Someone is definitely hiding what really happened around my father’s death. 

It's just like when people try to cover up a data breach. You know? Companies do it all the time. They get hacked, customer data gets stolen, and instead of just coming clean, they try to sweep it under the rug. They'll release a statement at 5:00 PM on a Friday before a long weekend, hoping the news cycle just buries it. We call it the Friday news dump. It's a classic PR move. 

I actually read this fascinating article about how PR firms handle crisis management. It's almost like a science. They have these whole playbooks for how to deflect blame and control the narrative. It made me think about getting into cybersecurity consulting, honestly. The money is insane, and you basically just get paid to tell companies how terrible their security posture is. I had a buddy who did that, and he was flying first class to London like twice a month. He said the jet lag was brutal, though. He had to start taking melatonin just to sleep. I tried melatonin once, but it gave me the weirdest, most vivid dreams. Like, I dreamt I was trapped in a giant maze made entirely of old server racks, and all the cables were tangled together like spaghetti. 

Cable management is a huge pet peeve of mine, by the way. If you look behind my desk, every single wire is zip-tied and routed perfectly. It's just so much easier to troubleshoot when you know exactly where everything goes. But yeah... there's no doubt in my mind. The evidence is right there if you actually look at it. They're definitely covering it up.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the fixed belief is encapsulated and non-bizarre, which would help distinguish delusional disorder from psychotic, stress-related, obsessive, or personality-based explanations.
doctor.question: Aside from your father’s death, do you have any other strong beliefs that other people say aren’t true?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient has any other strong beliefs or delusions (besides the one about the father's death). The symptom profile only describes the specific delusion regarding the father's death and does not contain information about other delusions.

patient.answer:
No, not really. I mean, the stuff with my dad is the only thing where people seem to think I'm... you know, off base. I'm a pretty logical guy otherwise. 

Although, I guess my coworkers think I'm totally crazy for my opinions on mechanical keyboards. Like, at work, everyone just uses those cheap, mushy membrane keyboards that come free with the desktop towers. It's terrible for your wrists and your typing speed. I brought in my own custom board with Cherry MX Blue switches—they're the really loud, tactile, clicky ones. My cubicle neighbor, Dave, actually filed an informal complaint with our manager because he said the typing noise was driving him insane. We got into this huge debate about office etiquette. I just told him he should invest in some decent noise-canceling headphones. 

I have a pair of Sonys, the XM4s, and they are literally life-changing. I snagged them during a Prime Day sale last year. Amazon's dynamic pricing algorithm is actually fascinating if you ever look into it. Sometimes if you leave something in your cart for a few days, the system automatically drops the price by a few bucks just to incentivize you to check out. It's all automated through machine learning models. We're actually starting to use some basic AI tools for log analysis at work and it’s... 

Wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, other beliefs. No, no. Just the evidence about my dad. That's it.
